title: Demonstrate knowledge of the legislation and regulations that are necessary for the exportation of perishable produce

lessons.title: The export industry and its supply chain
lessons.html:
Background of the perishable produce export industry

South Africa has exported fresh fruit for well over a century, starting with shipments of deciduous fruit from the Western Cape to Britain. For much of the twentieth century, exports were controlled by statutory marketing boards and single-channel exporters. After deregulation of agricultural marketing in the late 1990s, many independent exporters entered the market, and growers could choose who exported their fruit. Today the industry exports citrus, table grapes, apples, pears, stone fruit, avocados, mangoes, litchis, berries and vegetables to markets worldwide, and it is a major source of jobs and foreign exchange, especially in rural areas.

Because exporting is now open to many players, legislation plays an important role in keeping standards consistent so that the reputation of South African produce is protected.

The supply chain and its role-players

Role-playerRole
Producer (grower)Grows the crop according to GAP; registers production units
PackhouseGrades, treats, packs and marks the fruit; registered with a packhouse code
Cold storeCools and stores fruit before shipment
Exporter / marketing agentSells fruit to overseas buyers, arranges logistics and documents
TransporterMoves fruit by refrigerated truck to the port or airport
Port terminal and shipping lineHandles containers or pallets and carries them by sea
PPECBExport inspection and cold chain control
Department of AgricultureSets standards and phytosanitary requirements; issues phytosanitary certification
Industry associationsCGA, Hortgro, SATI, Subtrop: research, market access, information
Importer and retailerReceives, ripens, distributes and sells the fruit

Each link has legal duties. A mistake at one link, such as a missing packhouse code on a carton, can stop the whole consignment at the port.

lessons.title: The APS Act and the PPECB Act
lessons.html:
The Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990

The APS Act provides for control over the sale and export of certain agricultural products, so that minimum quality standards are maintained. Under this Act, regulations set export standards and requirements for regulated products such as fresh fruit. These regulations cover:

  • Quality: classes, maturity requirements and tolerances for defects.
  • Packing: types of containers, packing methods and net mass.
  • Marking: what must appear on cartons, such as product, cultivar, class, count or size, packer or exporter identification, and production unit and packhouse codes.
  • Inspection: products may only be exported after they have been inspected and approved.

The Department of Agriculture administers the Act and can appoint an assignee to carry out inspections. For fresh produce exports, PPECB acts as the assignee and inspects consignments before export.

The Perishable Products Export Control Act 9 of 1983

The PPECB Act established the Perishable Products Export Control Board. Its role includes:

  • controlling the export of perishable products in an orderly way;
  • ensuring perishable products are handled, cooled, stored and transported correctly to keep their quality;
  • approving and monitoring cold stores, containers and vessels used for perishable exports;
  • issuing cold chain related certificates and providing services such as temperature monitoring;
  • charging statutory levies or fees on exports to fund its work.

In practice, PPECB inspectors visit packhouses and cold stores, sample consignments, check temperatures and issue the approval that allows the fruit to be loaded. Exporters must register with PPECB and follow its cold chain instructions.

The two Acts work together: the APS Act sets what the product must look like and how it must be packed and marked; the PPECB Act ensures it stays in that condition all the way to the ship.

lessons.title: Special market requirements
lessons.html:
How special market requirements influence exports

Beyond South Africa's own standards, each importing country or buyer may add special requirements. These can decide whether a market is open at all and how much it costs to supply.

Phytosanitary requirements

  • Importing countries protect their agriculture from foreign pests and diseases.
  • They may require registered orchards and packhouses, pest monitoring, specific treatments such as cold treatment, and inspection by the national plant protection organisation before a phytosanitary certificate is issued.
  • Some markets, for example the USA, China and others, have bilateral protocols that list exactly what must be done for each fruit.

Food safety and residue requirements

  • Each market sets its own maximum residue limits (MRLs). A product legal in South Africa may have a lower MRL overseas.
  • Retailers may set limits even lower than the law and limit the number of different residues.

Private and ethical standards

  • GLOBALG.A.P. or equivalent farm certification.
  • Food safety schemes for packhouses.
  • Ethical and social audits covering labour practices, such as SIZA.
  • Environmental and sustainability requirements, such as water use and carbon footprint.

Packaging and labelling

  • Language, labelling and barcode requirements of the retailer.
  • Packaging materials, such as wood treatment or recyclable packaging.

Effect on exports

Special requirements increase costs and complexity, but they also create value: compliant fruit gets access to premium markets. An exporter planning to enter a new market must find out the requirements a season or more ahead, register orchards and packhouses, and train staff.

Key points

  • The export industry was deregulated in the late 1990s and now has many exporters.
  • The supply chain runs from grower to retailer, with PPECB and the Department of Agriculture as regulators.
  • The APS Act 119 of 1990 sets quality, packing, marking and inspection requirements.
  • The PPECB Act 9 of 1983 controls the export cold chain and established PPECB.
  • Special market requirements include phytosanitary protocols, MRLs and private standards.
